body: Recently, analysts have argued that emerging technologies with military applications may undermine nuclear stability (see here, here, and here), but the logic of these arguments is debatable and overlooks a more straightforward reason why new technology might cause nuclear conflict: by upending the existing balance of power among nuclear-armed states. This latter concern is more probable and dangerous and demands an immediate policy response.

For more than 70 years, the world has avoided major power conflict, and many attribute this era of peace to nuclear weapons. In situations of mutually assured destruction (MAD), neither side has an incentive to start a conflict because doing so will only result in its own annihilation. The key to this model of deterrence is the maintenance of secure second-strike capabilities—the ability to absorb an enemy nuclear attack and respond with a devastating counterattack.

Recently analysts have begun to worry, however, that new strategic military technologies may make it possible for a state to conduct a successful first strike on an enemy. For example, Chinese colleagues have complained to me in Track II dialogues that the United States may decide to launch a sophisticated cyberattack against Chinese nuclear command and control, essentially turning off China’s nuclear forces. Then, Washington will follow up with a massive strike with conventional cruise and hypersonic missiles to destroy China’s nuclear weapons. Finally, if any Chinese forces happen to survive, the United States can simply mop up China’s ragged retaliatory strike with advanced missile defenses. China will be disarmed and US nuclear weapons will still be sitting on the shelf, untouched.

If the United States, or any other state acquires such a first-strike capability, then the logic of MAD would be undermined. Washington may be tempted to launch a nuclear first strike. Or China may choose instead to use its nuclear weapons early in a conflict before they can be wiped out—the so-called “use ‘em or lose ‘em” problem.
According to this logic, therefore, the appropriate policy response would be to ban outright or control any new weapon systems that might threaten second-strike capabilities.

This way of thinking about new technology and stability, however, is open to question. Would any US president truly decide to launch a massive, bolt-out-of-the-blue nuclear attack because he or she thought s/he could get away with it? And why does it make sense for the country in the inferior position, in this case China, to intentionally start a nuclear war that it will almost certainly lose? More important, this conceptualization of how new technology affects stability is too narrow, focused exclusively on how new military technologies might be used against nuclear forces directly.

Rather, we should think more broadly about how new technology might affect global politics, and, for this, it is helpful to turn to scholarly international relations theory. The dominant theory of the causes of war in the academy is the “bargaining model of war.” This theory identifies rapid shifts in the balance of power as a primary cause of conflict.

International politics often presents states with conflicts that they can settle through peaceful bargaining, but when bargaining breaks down, war results. Shifts in the balance of power are problematic because they undermine effective bargaining. After all, why agree to a deal today if your bargaining position will be stronger tomorrow? And, a clear understanding of the military balance of power can contribute to peace. (Why start a war you are likely to lose?) But shifts in the balance of power muddy understandings of which states have the advantage.
You may see where this is going. New technologies threaten to create potentially destabilizing shifts in the balance of power.

For decades, stability in Europe and Asia has been supported by US military power. In recent years, however, the balance of power in Asia has begun to shift, as China has increased its military capabilities. Already, Beijing has become more assertive in the region, claiming contested territory in the South China Sea. And the results of Russia’s military modernization have been on full display in its ongoing intervention in Ukraine.

Moreover, China may have the lead over the United States in emerging technologies that could be decisive for the future of military acquisitions and warfare, including 3D printing, hypersonic missiles, quantum computing, 5G wireless connectivity, and artificial intelligence (AI). And Russian President Vladimir Putin is building new unmanned vehicles while ominously declaring, “Whoever leads in AI will rule the world.”

If China or Russia are able to incorporate new technologies into their militaries before the United States, then this could lead to the kind of rapid shift in the balance of power that often causes war.

If Beijing believes emerging technologies provide it with a newfound, local military advantage over the United States, for example, it may be more willing than previously to initiate conflict over Taiwan. And if Putin thinks new tech has strengthened his hand, he may be more tempted to launch a Ukraine-style invasion of a NATO member.

Either scenario could bring these nuclear powers into direct conflict with the United States, and once nuclear armed states are at war, there is an inherent risk of nuclear conflict through limited nuclear war strategies, nuclear brinkmanship, or simple accident or inadvertent escalation.

This framing of the problem leads to a different set of policy implications. The concern is not simply technologies that threaten to undermine nuclear second-strike capabilities directly, but, rather, any technologies that can result in a meaningful shift in the broader balance of power. And the solution is not to preserve second-strike capabilities, but to preserve prevailing power balances more broadly.

When it comes to new technology, this means that the United States should seek to maintain an innovation edge. Washington should also work with other states, including its nuclear-armed rivals, to develop a new set of arms control and nonproliferation agreements and export controls to deny these newer and potentially destabilizing technologies to potentially hostile states.
These are no easy tasks, but the consequences of [the US] Washington losing the race for technological superiority to its autocratic challengers just might mean nuclear [war] Armageddon.
Nuclear war leads to extinction
Ruff ’24

[Tilman Ruff; Associate professor in the University of Melbourne’s Nossal Institute for Global Health. Given the Nobel Peace Prize for drawing attention to the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of use of nuclear weapons and its efforts to achieve a treaty-based prohibition of such weapons; 2024; “Nuclear Weapons, Climate Disruption and Planetary Health”; University of Melbourne; https://doi.org/10.1079/9781800620025.0003]

This chapter explores the acute existential threat that nuclear weapons pose to humankind and the biosphere, including the global climate. If not eliminated first, they will destroy civilization, catastrophically damage the biosphere and risk extinction for humans and many other species. Fewer than 2% of the devices in the current global nuclear arsenal, if exploded on cities, would cause a[n]brupt ice age conditions, putting over 2 billion people at risk of starvation. The 2017 UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons provides the best available pathway for all nations to fulfill their obligation to eliminate nuclear weapons. Scientists and health professionals have vital roles and responsibilities in work to end nuclear weapons.
3.1 Context: Existential Threats

Collisions of sizeable celestial bodies with planet Earth have been responsible for most major extinction events, such as that of the dinosaurs 65 million years ago. We may now be able to anticipate and avoid many such catastrophic collisions and should work collectively to improve these capabilities. In billions of years we can expect our Sun to expand into a red giant star and render the Earth uninhabitable.

However, there are two other kinds of unprecedented existential threats which have emerged recently and are of human origin. Though they are upon us, it is not yet too late to take the urgent decisive preventive action they demand. The first is the subject of much of this book: environmental disruption, degradation and depletion of vital resources and ecosystems. Poorly controlled global heating poses the greatest of these interrelated challenges. The second, more acute and potentially less reversible, is the danger of nuclear war.

The World Health Assembly, the pre-eminent annual meeting of the World Health Organization (WHO), identified nuclear weapons as the greatest immediate threat to human health and welfare (WHO, 1983). The modest, often minimal, attention generally given to this issue by health professionals, including in their training and organizations, as for many other professions, is starkly at odds with this reality. Preventing use of nuclear weapons, by accident or design, necessitates their eradication – an urgent and feasible precondition for securing and sustaining planetary and human survival and health. Two senior climate scientists recently wrote: ‘We must solve the problem of nuclear weapons so that we have the luxury of devoting our time to solving the climate crisis’ (Robock and Prager, 2021).
3.2 What Nuclear Weapons Do

Evidence of the true extent of the effects of nuclear weapons has frequently not been collected, or has been covered up, misrepresented or disregarded by governments, to reinforce the myths that nuclear weapons are weapons like any other, only bigger, and can be used to serve legitimate military purposes and enhance security (Ruff, 2013). Public acceptance of the massive investments and risks involved to develop, produce, deploy and threaten to use nuclear weapons depends on an understanding of their effects that is not firmly based on evidence of what nuclear weapons actually do. No meaningful health or humanitarian response, reconciliation or recovery is possible after the catastrophic indiscriminate radioactive violence of a nuclear war. The concept of ‘winners’ would be meaningless; there would only be losers

The bomb that destroyed Hiroshima and killed 140,000 people in the first five months, and is still killing people 78 years later, was by today’s standards a small, tactical-size weapon, 15 kilotonnes (15 kt) of high-explosive equivalent. The average explosive power of the weapons in today’s arsenal is almost 11 times larger (162 kt); the biggest nuclear weapon deployed currently at 5 megatonnes (5 Mt) is more than 330 times larger. A single nuclear weapon (in Russia in 1961) has been detonated with more than four times the destructive power of all explosives used in all wars throughout human history.
Acute effects

The effects of nuclear weapons differ both quantitatively and qualitatively from those of any other weapon (Table 3.1). Nuclear weapons produce an enormous blast wave that causes trauma both directly (such as lung trauma and eardrum rupture), and indirectly through powerful winds that can turn objects, including people, into missiles. An intense flash of light and initial ionizing radiation are produced together with intense heat, which causes direct vaporization, incineration and burns, and ignites anything flammable over a large area

Apart from their essentially limitless destructive power, a defining feature of nuclear weapons is the release of huge amounts of radioactivity in the initial pulse as well as radioactive fallout containing hundreds of different radioisotopes with half-lives ranging from fractions of a second to millions of years. Fallout is dispersedby wind and water over great distances, eventually worldwide. Ionizing radiation causes acute toxicity to many organs (acute radiation sickness) at high doses; and in the long term, at any level, causes dose-related and heritable genetic damage and subsequent lifelong increased risk of cancer and chronic disease.

An intense burst of radiowaves produced by a nuclear explosion (electromagnetic pulse) (EMP) would cause extensive disruption of electrical equipment. The EMP from a nuclear explosion high in the atmosphere would cover a continental-size area with voltage a million times greater than lightning. Some military equipment is specifically hardened against such an effect; virtually all civilian equipment, including electricity grids, is not. An EMP would disrupt the vast array of electrical and electronic equipment on which the infrastructure of modern societies is increasingly dependent – including electricity and water supply, telecommunications, computer systems, transport networks, medical equipment, the internet, cars and trucks, traffic lights, banking, appliances, and most commerce and trade

The largest nuclear weapons currently deployed are 5 Mt – the equivalent amount of high explosive would fill a freight train 2414 km long. The energy released by such a bomb could turn 5 Mt of ice to steam. Within a thousandth of a second, conditions akin to the centre of the Sun would be produced: 100 × 106 °C and 100 × 106 atmospheres of pressure in a fireball which would rapidly expand to 1.8 km across. Within 4.7 km in every direction, winds of 750 km/h and a blast wave over 140 kilopascals (kPa) would crush, collapse, or explode all buildings, including those of steel and reinforced concrete, and turn the debris into missiles with lethal velocity. Glass and steel would melt; concrete would explode. Wherever they were, all living things would die almost immediately – vaporized, crushed, charred, irradiated.

Out to about 7.5 km in every direction, winds of 460 km/h and blast pressures of 80 kPa would break apart concrete and steel buildings and sweep out their walls, floors, and ceilings. Aluminium would be vaporized. Adults would be hurled over 100 m at high speed. Essentially everyone would be killed or seriously injured, including by crush injuries, penetrating wounds, ruptured lungs and other internal organs, transected spinal cords and nerves, severe haemorrhage and deep burns.

As far as 12.3 km in every direction, winds of 260 km/h and blast pressures of 35 kPa would crush wooden and brick buildings, including houses, schools, shops and many factories. People would be hurled 7 m. Asphalt would melt. Windows would be fragmented into more than 4000 projectile glass shards per square metre. Many people would be deaf from ruptured eardrums. In less than 10 seconds a city would be completely devastated.

Stretching 22.6 km in every direction, over an area of 1605 km2, everything flammable would ignite – wood, paper, cloth, vegetation, plastics, petrol, and oil from ruptured tanks and cars; further fuelled by ruptured gas pipes, downed electricity lines and leaking chemicals. Within half an hour, thousands upon thousands of fires would coalesce into a giant firestorm 45 km across, with temperatures of more than 800°C, sucking in air and creating winds of more than 320 km/h, consuming available oxygen. Within this area, every living thing would die and shelters would become crematoria.

Still further out, windows would be shattered, buildings damaged, broken debris turned into projectiles. Streets would be impassable. There would be no functioning ambulances, paramedics, fire engines or police, no power or communications or functioning hospitals. The vast majority of injured and burnt people would die alone without so much as a hand or voice to comfort them and without any relief for their agonizing pain.

Smaller weapons in the range of tens to hundreds of kilotonnes are about 100 times more efficient per kilotonne of explosive force at killing people and igniting fires compared with megatonne-range weapons (Toon et al., 2007).
WHO reports

In 1983, the World Health Assembly considered the first report of an international committee of experts on the effects of nuclear war on health and health services, coordinated by WHO. It endorsed the committee’s conclusion ‘that it is impossible to prepare health services to deal in any systematic way with the catastrophe resulting from nuclear warfare, and that nuclear weapons constitute the greatest immediate threat to the health and welfare of mankind’ (WHO, 1983). The committee’s report stated: ‘It is obvious that no health service in any area of the world would be capable of dealing adequately with the hundreds of thousands of people seriously injured by blast, heat or radiation from even a single 1-megatonne bomb.’ The committee concluded that: ‘the only approach to the treatment of the health effects of nuclear explosions is primary prevention of such explosions, that is, the primary prevention of atomic war’ (WHO, 1983, pp. 5–6).

WHO issued an updated report in 1987, including new research on urban superfires caused by nuclear explosions, concluding that deaths caused by such fires could be 3–4 times greater than those caused by blast (WHO, 1987). The report also considered the emerging evidence of global climate impact – nuclear winter – that would follow nuclear war even involving only a small fraction of the global arsenal detonated over large fuel-dense modern cities. It concluded: ‘After a major nuclear war famine and diseaseswould be widespread and social, communication and economic systems around the world would be disrupted’ (WHO, 1987, p. 5).
3.3 New Evidence of Climate Impacts

In the decades since, we have learned much about the multiplicity of impacts of nuclear explosions and war. The evidence grows ever clearer as to the catastrophic effects. With striking consistency, the more we learn, the worse are the assessed impacts of nuclear war. New evidence on the health impacts of ionizing radiation demonstrates greater and more diverse impacts than previously understood; it confirms the lack of a threshold dose for adverse health effects, shows that a dose rate reduction factor should not be applied, and confirms increased risk at all doses for a range of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), particularly cardiovascular disease (Ruff, 2017; Little et al., 2023). Field studies of a wide range of plants and animals in the contaminated regions around Chernobyl and Fukushima demonstrate extremely pervasive effects, from genetic and individual developmental, phenotypic, fitness and fertility impacts, to population, species and ecosystem effects, far greater than those expected based on in vitro studies (Mousseau, 2021).

Major humanitarian organizations, including the Red Cross Red Crescent movement and UN agencies, have re-examined capacities nationally and globally to respond to nuclear detonations, and concluded, as WHO did in the 1980s, that no capacity exists or is feasible to respond meaningfully to humanitarian needs in the aftermath of even a single nuclear detonation in a city.

However, the most important new evidence relates to climate impacts. Nuclear weapons are extremely efficient at igniting vast numbers of simultaneous fires over large areas. These would consume all flammable materials and coalesce into massive confluent fires within which no one could survive the > 800°C heat, intense smoke and oxygen depletion. Atmospheric scientists estimated that even the relatively small tactical-size nuclear weapon exploded on Hiroshima (15 kt of high-explosive equivalent) released about 1000 times as much energy in the fires it ignited as in the explosion itself (Toon et al., 2007). In Hiroshima approximately 13 km2 of the city burned completely. As described above, detonation of the largest currently deployed nuclear weapon, up to 5 Mt in size, would engulf a city in a confluent megafire more than 45 km in diameter, 1600 km2 in area (Ruff, 2013).
Atmospheric and climate effects of regional nuclear war: the example of India–Pakistan

The scenario for regional nuclear war most often studied by atmospheric scientists is a war between India and Pakistan. This possibility is all too realistic, as the two nations have waged war four times since their independence in 1949, and mobilized up to 1 million troops on two further occasions. Violence erupts across their disputed border in Kashmir almost daily. They possess two of the world’s six growing nuclear arsenals. Both have policies that create high risks of nuclear escalation in a war between them. The most recently updated scenario involves use of 250 nuclear weapons of 15, 50, or 100 kt in size, half the combined arsenal they were estimated on current trajectory to possess in 2025 (Toon et al., 2019). These constitute 2% of the number of nuclear weapons worldwide and amount to less than 1% of their explosive yield, because the average size of the current 12,119 nuclear weapons is 162 kt (Kristensen et al., 2024).

Such a war would produce between 83 and 183 million acute casualties in cities across both nations, including 52–127 million deaths, depending on the size of the weapons used. Radioactive contamination, severe social and economic disruption, and people attempting to flee on an unprecedented scale would extend across South Asia and beyond. Such a war would also produce between 16 and 37 Mt of black carbon in sooty smoke from burning cities (Toon et al., 2019). This smoke would loftquickly into the upper stratosphere and mesosphere, beyond the reach of clouds and precipitation in the lower atmosphere (troposphere). The sun would heat the rising smoke by 50–80°C, lofting and keeping it high in the atmosphere, where it would blanket the Earth for over a decade. It would reduce global average surface temperatures by 3–6°C, well within the range of minimum temperatures during the peak of the last ice age 20,000 years ago, 3–8°C colder than present. Unevenly distributed temperature declines of 8–15°C would cover much of the large North American and Eurasian land masses where most of the world’s grain is grown.

Global precipitation would also decline by up to 40%, with particular disruption of the South Asian monsoon on which food production for 1.5 billion people critically depends. Incident sunlight would decline by up to 30%. Scientists expect these darker, drier conditions and colder temperatures to be associated with cold spellsand shorter frost-free growing seasons in temperate regions. An unprecedented increase in ultraviolet flux (30–100% increases during summer outside the tropics) would exacerbate these changes (Mills et al., 2015). Stratospheric ozone would be extensively depleted in the hot smoky stratosphere, with harmful effects of increased ultraviolet (UV) radiation on plant and animal development and health in both aquatic and terrestrial environments. Even a smaller India–Pakistan nuclear war releasing 5 Mt of soot would produce peak global ozone loss of 25%, and up to 55% loss at higher latitudes, leading to a peak increase of 40% in the UVB wavelengths associated with DNA damage, with recovery taking 12 years (Bardeen et al., 2021). Most agricultural production would abruptly cease in higher-latitude regions, including Canada, northern areas of Europe, Russia, China, Korea and Japan (Jägermeyr et al., 2020)

Radioactive fallout and toxic chemical contamination from damaged pipelines and industrial and storage sites would affect large areas of agricultural land. Social, economic, transport and trade turmoil would disrupt global distribution of fertilizer, fuel, machinery and equipment, parts, seeds, pesticides, food storage facilities, and transport on which modern agriculture, food storage and distribution depend. The direct climatic changes alone would cause a decline in net primary productivity (NPP) of between 10% and 20% in the oceans and between 15% and 40% on land over multiple years (Toon et al., 2019). NPP is the net amount of carbon per square metre per year converted into plant matter after accounting for what plants use for their own respiration. This loss would be comparable to the total current annual human use of food and fibre. Agricultural losses could not be offset by the world’s fisheries, especially with preexisting widespread overfishing as occurs currently (Scherrer et al., 2020).

Scientists continue to discover new effects that would exacerbate the harm. Recent findings indicate that various nuclear war scenarios could induce an El Niño-like pattern of unprecedented magnitude across the Pacific, with associated reductions in equatorial Pacific phytoplankton productivity of about 40% (Coupe et al., 2021). Researchers recently identified large and abrupt exacerbations in global ocean acidification as a consequence of nuclear conflict, including potential inability for marine calcifying organisms like shellfish and corals to maintain their shells or skeletons in a corrosive environment (Lovenduski et al., 2020). Even the smallest nuclear war would devastate ocean systems, leading to sharp declines in fish stocks, expansion of ice sheets into coastal communities and changes in ocean currents that would take decades or longer to reverse (Harrison et al., 2022). Sea temperature impacts from nuclear war are particularly extreme in coastal regions where the majority of fish catch and marine ecosystem services are provided. Entirely different conditions for nutrients vital to plankton at the base of food chain would be widespread through the world’s oceans. Some nuclear little ice age changes are likely to last hundreds of years or longer (Harrison et al., 2022).
Nutritional impact

The world is ill prepared to withstand any sustained and substantial decline in food production. In July 2022, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations (UN) estimated between 702 and 828 million people faced hunger in 2021, 150 million more than in 2019 (FAO et al., 2022). Worsened by the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, FAO estimated the number of people experiencing moderate or severe food insecurity in 2021 at 2.31 billion. The Global Report on Food Crises 2023 estimated that the number of people facing high levels of food insecurity has increased from 105 million people in 48 countries in 2016, to 258 million people in 58 countries in 2022 (FSIN and GNAFC, 2023). The FAO forecast for the year 2022/23 for global cereal stocks is equivalent to about 112 days of consumption (FAO, 2023).

It has been known for decades that extrapolation of the physical effects of nuclear detonations cannot begin to characterize the reality of the world after nuclear war, and that the climatic effects of nuclear war and disruption of global food support systems could result in the deaths of multiple billion humans (Harwell et al., 1989; Helfand et al., 2016). Recent work has provided more detailed global and countryspecific estimates of the impacts of regional and global nuclear war on both terrestrial and aquatic food production and nutrition (Xia et al., 2022). Soot injections greater than 5 Mt, as would be produced by burning cities ignited by 100 Hiroshima size nuclear explosions, would lead to mass food shortages. In the three scenarios described above for an India–Pakistan war utilizing 250 nuclear weapons 15, 50 or 100 kt in yield, with 16–37 Mt of smoke, the number of people estimated to die of starvation by the end of the second year after such a war would range between 926 million and 2.081 billion – more than 16 times the number of direct fatalities. Food stores, livestock and aquatic food production would be unable to compensate for persistently reduced crop output. Adaptation measures such as killing livestock and reducing food waste would have quite limited impact. Crop reduction and starvation would be most severe in mid and high northern latitudes. For example, assuming livestock has been slaughtered and animal feed diverted to human consumption, an India– Pakistan war producing 37 Mt of smoke would result, after two years, in the starvation of over a billion people in China, 125 million in Russia, 131 million in the USA and 39 million in the UK.

These salutory estimates are nevertheless quite conservative, as they used an FAO database reflecting a global population of 6.7 rather than the current 8 billion; they do not account for direct or radiation-related deaths, increased solar ultraviolet radiation, disruption of agricultural inputs, food storage and distribution, displacement, societal collapse or conflict, electromagnetic pulse effects, or contamination of productive land by radiation and chemical pollution.

Epidemics of various infectious diseases would inevitably accompany famine of such unprecedented magnitude, as well as conflict within and between nations over unequal, inadequate and rapidly diminishing food reserves. The combination would likely substantially exacerbate the human toll. Human civilization would not be expected to survive a shock of this magnitude.
Effects of a Russia–USA nuclear war

Nuclear war utilizing a substantial portion of the deployed Russian and US nuclear arsenals is conservatively estimated to produce 150 Mt ofblack carbon in smoke from burning cities. Over the course of a week, this would plummet global surface temperatures to more than 9°C colder than present, with temperatures in extensive areas of the Eurasian and North American land masses dropping by 20–35°C, and locations such as Ukraine and Iowa barely experiencing days with minimum temperatures above freezing for two years (Coupe et al., 2019). Such a severe nuclear winter would put the survival of humans and many other species in severe jeopardy. For a war between Russia and the USA using 4400 nuclear weapons 100 kt in size, less than half their weapons stockpile, over 5 billion people would be expected to succumb to famine by the end of year 2. In the most favourable livestock and food waste scenario for human survival, by the end of year 2 more than 99% of the population of China, Canada and northern Europe would be starving, along with more than 75% of the population of Russia and the USA (Xia et al., 2022).
